bullets.text: The three-designers story holds idea quality constant to compare the leverage of screens, strategy, and a live demo.
Its executive perspective rewards decision support and shareable execution over tenure or basic AI usage.
The cited surveys distinguish widespread AI use from worker competence and organizational maturity.
Ambitious spending plans coexist with employee apprehension and limited enterprise-wide financial impact.
The ladder distinguishes default-tool use, custom workflow integration, and invention of new AI capabilities.
Its economic claim is that greater command of AI produces leverage that can harden into wealth.

sections.label: Adaptive skills, not just superstar talent

bullets.text: Wage and productivity figures support a widening premium for applying AI fluently within ordinary roles.
Researcher pay sits at the apex; the broader prescription is continual upskilling rather than a research career.
The essay contrasts being managed by algorithms with authoring the workflows that allocate value.
Its three routes upward combine control over defaults, ongoing learning, and choosing worthwhile problems.
The ending recommends an apprenticeship mindset: keep revising workflows and prompts rather than treating fluency as permanent.

notes.text: The exercise controls for idea quality by assumption, then judges deliverables by executive usefulness. Read the retention verdict as a claim about organizational leverage, not proof that static design work is intrinsically worse.

The passage pairs ambitious spending plans with limited maturity and employee apprehension. Is the bottleneck individual skill, organizational support, or the ability to translate experimentation into shared workflows?

The wage premium and faster skill turnover pull in opposite directions: fluency can earn more, but its content keeps changing. The moat described here depends on repeated adaptation, not a credential acquired once.
The invoice example makes a stronger claim than time saved: the builder helps define what counts as reconciled. This is why the essay links AI literacy to decision rights, not simply higher output.
